steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on EyeTrans, which brings human attention from eye-tracking data into Transformer attention for neural code summarization. It should cover code summaries and programmer attention, eye-tracking studies, machine attention in code summarization models, what we did and found, our contributions, and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Code summaries and programmer attention
2. Eye-tracking studies of human attention in code comprehension and summarization
3. Machine attention, Transformer models for code summarization, open questions
4. This paper: EyeTrans, human study, two evaluation tasks, results
5. Contributions
6. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Code summaries
- code summary = brief description of purpose and function of code; aids developer comprehension
- common part of documentation; usually written by developer, ML models increasingly generate them automatically
- when summarizing, programmers' attention focuses on different parts of code -> general idea -> comprehensive understanding

2. Eye-tracking studies
- several studies on how human developers comprehend code
- popular approach: eye-tracking studies, analyze common eye gaze patterns
- certain gaze patterns = change in attention within code; correlated with changes in concentration; valuable for understanding cognitive processes in programming
- eye-tracking studies on code summarization: university students / professional developers drafting or evaluating summaries, gaze recorded
- focus mostly on understanding patterns, but found correlations between visual attention and code summarization -> future tool design using human attention

3. Machine attention
- "attention" in ML: importance of weights in layers of neural networks
- Transformer: one of most influential baseline structures with neural attention
- advances in machine attention for system applications; more Transformer-based models for neural code summarization
- domain knowledge modifies model structures: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), dataflow graph, function call graph
- these models try to "comprehend" code, as human programmers do -> human attention could improve them; not attempted yet (to our knowledge)
- questions: can human attention be integrated into machine attention to enhance performance? how to incorporate it pragmatically?
- relevant to SE and AI communities: Transformer underlies recent AI applications in SE and LLMs in NLP

4. EyeTrans
- hypothesis: human attention can enhance Transformer models; no formalized methodology yet
- EyeTrans uses human eye-tracking data during training (Figure 1)
- human study: eye-tracking data from 27 programmers; preprocess and incorporate into Transformer
- two evaluation methods:
  - (1) Functional Summarization: classification, predict function name (e.g. "open", "sort") from source code; foundational step
  - (2) General Code Summarization: seq2seq, generate natural language tokens describing what function does (e.g. documentation)
- results: up to 29.91% improvement in functional summarization, up to 6.39% in general code summarization
- proof-of-concept; hope to inspire human factor research in AI for SE
- de-identified eye-tracking data and code in supplementary package, to be released

5. Contributions
- EyeTrans: first approach showing human attention + Transformer substantially enhances neural code summarization
- exploratory examination of eye-tracking data, preliminary analysis
- data-centric method, no change to Transformer structure; quantitative analyses
- changes in Transformer attention maps (qualitative)
- review of attention synthesis methods; future avenues

6. Organization
- Sec 2 study design + background; Sec 3 EyeTrans details; Sec 4 experimental setup; Sec 5 results; Sec 6 threats to validity; Sec 7 related work; Sec 9 conclusion and future directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A code summary is a short description of what a piece of code does and what it is for, and it can help developers understand the code. Code summaries are a common part of documenting source code. Usually the developer writes them, but machine learning models are more and more being used to generate summaries automatically, to add to the documentation and help comprehension. When programmers document or summarize source code, their attention focuses on different parts of the code so they can get a general idea of it, and in the end they build a comprehensive understanding of it.

Several studies have started to understand how human developers comprehend code. A popular way to capture how programmers' attention shifts when they read code is to do eye-tracking studies and empirically analyze the common eye gaze patterns during the process. Intuitively, some eye gaze patterns when looking at source code correspond to a change in attention within the code. This is usually highly correlated with changes in human concentration, and it is potentially valuable for understanding the cognitive processes in programming better. Researchers have done several eye-tracking studies to explore human attention during code summarization. Usually university students or professional developers write or evaluate summaries for code snippets, and their eye gaze patterns are recorded to understand human attention in these activities. The focus has mainly been on understanding the eye-tracking patterns, but these studies have also found some correlations between human visual attention and code summarization. This opens the way for future work to improve tool design using human attention.

Besides the traditional meaning of "attention" in human activities, in recent years attention can also refer to a concept in machine learning, which describes the importance of weights in the layers of neural networks. In this area, the Transformer architecture is one of the most influential baseline structures that put neural attention into a machine learning model. With advances in machine attention mechanisms for system applications, more and more Transformer-based models have been developed for a variety of neural code summarization tasks. These methods use specific domain knowledge to change their model structures, adding things like the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), dataflow graph, and function call graph. To generate code summaries these Transformer models basically try to "comprehend" the code, which is something human programmers already do. So it is possible that human attention could be used to improve the performance of these models, and as far as we know nobody has tried this yet. We can put this as the following questions: can human attention be integrated into complex machine attention mechanisms to improve the overall performance? If it can, how can we incorporate human attention into attention-based machine learning models in a practical way? These questions are relevant for the Software Engineering (SE) and AI communities, because the Transformer architecture is what the most recent advanced AI applications in SE are built on, and also large language models (LLMs) in natural language processing (NLP).

4. EyeTrans
- hypothesis: human attention can enhance Transformer models; formalized methodology not yet explored -> EyeTrans
- uses human eye-tracking data during training to integrate human and machine attention (Figure 1)
- human study with 27 programmers; data preprocessed and incorporated into Transformer
- two evaluations: (1) Functional Summarization (classification, predict function name e.g. "open"/"sort"); (2) General Code Summarization (seq2seq, natural language description e.g. documentation)
- up to 29.91% better in functional summarization, up to 6.39% in general code summarization
- proof-of-concept; de-identified data + code in supplementary package, to be released

5. Contributions
- first approach showing human attention + Transformer enhances neural code summarization
- exploratory examination of eye-tracking data
- data-centric method without altering structure; quantitative analyses
- attention map changes (qualitative)
- review of attention synthesis methods, future avenues

6. Organization
- Sec 2 study design + background; Sec 3 EyeTrans; Sec 4 setup; Sec 5 results; Sec 6 threats; Sec 7 related work; Sec 9 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A code summary is a short description of what a piece of code does and what it is for, and it can help developers understand the code. Code summaries are a common part of documenting source code. Usually the developer writes them, but machine learning models are more and more being used to generate summaries automatically, to add to the documentation and help comprehension. When programmers document or summarize source code, their attention focuses on different parts of the code so they can get a general idea of it, and in the end they build a comprehensive understanding of it.

Several studies have started to understand how human developers comprehend code. A popular way to capture how programmers' attention shifts when they read code is to do eye-tracking studies and empirically analyze the common eye gaze patterns during the process. Intuitively, some eye gaze patterns when looking at source code correspond to a change in attention within the code. This is usually highly correlated with changes in human concentration, and it is potentially valuable for understanding the cognitive processes in programming better. Researchers have done several eye-tracking studies to explore human attention during code summarization. Usually university students or professional developers write or evaluate summaries for code snippets, and their eye gaze patterns are recorded to understand human attention in these activities. The focus has mainly been on understanding the eye-tracking patterns, but these studies have also found some correlations between human visual attention and code summarization. This opens the way for future work to improve tool design using human attention.

Besides the traditional meaning of "attention" in human activities, in recent years attention can also refer to a concept in machine learning, which describes the importance of weights in the layers of neural networks. In this area, the Transformer architecture is one of the most influential baseline structures that put neural attention into a machine learning model. With advances in machine attention mechanisms for system applications, more and more Transformer-based models have been developed for a variety of neural code summarization tasks. These methods use specific domain knowledge to change their model structures, adding things like the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), dataflow graph, and function call graph. To generate code summaries these Transformer models basically try to "comprehend" the code, which is something human programmers already do. So it is possible that human attention could be used to improve the performance of these models, and as far as we know nobody has tried this yet. We can put this as the following questions: can human attention be integrated into complex machine attention mechanisms to improve the overall performance? If it can, how can we incorporate human attention into attention-based machine learning models in a practical way? These questions are relevant for the Software Engineering (SE) and AI communities, because the Transformer architecture is what the most recent advanced AI applications in SE are built on, and also large language models (LLMs) in natural language processing (NLP).

In this paper, we hypothesize that human attention can improve Transformer models. A formalized methodology for this integration has not been explored yet, so we introduce EyeTrans. EyeTrans uses human eye-tracking data during training to integrate human attention with machine attention, as shown in Figure 1. To do this, we first do a human study to collect eye-tracking data from 27 programmers, and then we preprocess the data and incorporate it into the Transformer. We describe our methodology and then we present evaluation metrics to assess the performance of EyeTrans. We use two evaluation methods based on code summarization to show that human attention helps neural code summarization: (1) classification-based code summarization, which we call Functional Summarization, where a model predicts the name of a function (e.g., "open" or "sort") given its source code. This is a foundational step that lets programmers get a preliminary understanding of the functionality and semantics of the code. (2) Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) based code summarization, which we call General Code Summarization, where a model generates a sequence of natural language tokens that briefly describes what a given function does (e.g., documentation for the function). We find that integrating human attention improves performance by up to 29.91% in functional summarization and by up to 6.39% in general code summarization, which shows that EyeTrans is effective. We see our work as a proof-of-concept and we hope it can inspire more future work to use human factor research in AI for software engineering. The eye-tracking data collected in the study (de-identified) and the experimental code are included in the supplementary package, and we plan to release them to the public.

The contributions of this paper are:

- We propose EyeTrans, the first approach to show that integrating human attention with the Transformer architecture can substantially improve the performance of neural code summarization.

- We do exploratory examinations of the eye-tracking data and use a preliminary analysis to rationalize integrating human attention.

- We design a data-centric method to incorporate human attention into Transformers without changing their structure, and we present comprehensive quantitative analyses to validate the performance of the approach.

- We show changes in the Transformer's attention maps to qualitatively demonstrate what changes when human attention is combined with the attention layer in the Transformer.

- We review existing attention synthesis methods in relation to our work and outline possible directions for future research.

Paper Organization: Section 2 presents the design of the eye-tracking human study and gives background on EyeTrans and the Transformer architecture. Section 3 explains the details of EyeTrans. Section 4 gives the experimental setup. Section 5 analyzes the results. Section 6 discusses threats to validity. Section 7 surveys related work. Section 9 concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.

These typically involve university students or professional developers drafting or evaluating summaries for code snippets while their eye gaze patterns are recorded to understand human attention in such activities [11,12]. Though the focus has mainly been on understanding the eye-tracking patterns, these studies have revealed certain correlations between human visual attention and code summarization [4,3], paving the way for future work to improve tool design by leveraging human attention.

In recent years, alongside the traditional definition of "attention" in human activities, attention can also refer to a concept in machine learning that describes the importance of weights in the layers of neural networks [13,14]. Within this area, the Transformer [15] architecture is one of the most influential baseline structures incorporating neural attention into a machine learning model. With advancements in machine attention mechanisms for system applications [16,17,18], a growing number of Transformer-based models have been developed to address a variety of neural code summarization tasks [19,20,21,22]. These methods leverage specific domain knowledge to modify their model structures, incorporating elements such as the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) [19], dataflow graph [21], and function call graph [23]. To generate code summaries, these Transformer models essentially aim to "comprehend" the code, a task that human programmers already accomplish. It is therefore possible that human attention could be leveraged to improve these models' performance [24], which, to the best of our knowledge, has not yet been attempted. This can be framed as the following questions: can human attention be integrated into complex machine attention mechanisms to enhance overall performance? If so, how can we pragmatically incorporate human attention into attention-based machine learning models? These questions are particularly relevant for the Software Engineering (SE) and AI communities given the Transformer architecture, which underlies the most recent advanced AI applications in SE, and large language models (LLMs) in natural language processing (NLP) [25,26,27].

In this paper, we hypothesize that human attention can enhance Transformer models, and since a formalized methodology for this integration has yet to be explored, we introduce EyeTrans. EyeTrans leverages human eye-tracking data during training to integrate human attention with machine attention, as illustrated in Figure 1. To this end, we first conduct a human study to collect eye-tracking data from 27 programmers, which we then preprocess and incorporate into the Transformer. We describe our methodology, then present evaluation metrics that assess EyeTrans's performance. Specifically, we employ two code summarization-based evaluation methods to illustrate the effectiveness of human attention in augmenting neural code summarization: (1) classification-based code summarization, referred to as Functional Summarization, in which a model predicts the name of a function (e.g., "open" or "sort") given its source code. This serves as a foundational step that lets programmers consolidate a preliminary understanding of the functionality and semantics of the code. (2) Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) based code summarization, referred to as General Code Summarization, in which a model generates a sequence of natural language tokens briefly describing what a given function does (e.g., documentation for the function). We find that integrating human attention improves performance by up to 29.91% in functional summarization and up to 6.39% in general code summarization, demonstrating the effectiveness of EyeTrans. We view our work as a proof-of-concept and hope it can inspire more future work leveraging human factor research in AI for software engineering. We include the eye-tracking data collected in the study (de-identified) and the experimental code in the supplementary package and plan to release them to the public.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

- We propose EyeTrans, the first approach to demonstrate that integrating human attention with the Transformer architecture can substantially enhance the performance of neural code summarization.

- We conduct exploratory examinations of eye-tracking data and rationalize the integration of human attention through a preliminary analysis.

- We design a data-centric method to incorporate human attention into Transformers without altering their structure, and present comprehensive quantitative analyses to validate the performance of our approach.

- We illustrate changes in the Transformer's attention maps to qualitatively demonstrate the effect of combining human attention with the attention layer in the Transformer.

- We review existing attention synthesis methods in relation to our work and outline future avenues of research.

Paper Organization: Section 2 presents the design of the eye-tracking human study and provides background on EyeTrans and the Transformer architecture. Section 3 describes the details of EyeTrans. Section 4 details the experimental setup. Section 5 analyzes the results. Section 6 discusses threats to validity. Section 7 surveys related work. Finally, Section 9 concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.
